# Writing Style Guide {.unnumbered}

This guide describes Shea's preferred format for manuscript drafts. These preferences reflect his experience as an author, reviewer, and mentor; they are house style, not universal rules. Following them makes drafts easier to review and keeps collaborators from spending time on avoidable formatting changes.

## Order of precedence

Use the following order when requirements differ:

1. **Target journal:** Follow the current author instructions for the journal where the manuscript will be submitted.
2. **Default journal:** If the target journal has not been selected or does not address an issue, follow the [*Alzheimer's & Dementia* author guidelines](https://alz-journals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/hub/journal/15525279/homepage/author-guidelines).
3. **Lab house style:** Use the preferences below when neither set of journal instructions answers the question.

For example, Shea prefers justified text and 1.5-line spacing in working drafts. *Alzheimer's & Dementia*, however, requests left-aligned, double-spaced manuscripts. Use the journal's requirements when preparing that submission.

::: {.callout-important}
Check the target journal's instructions again immediately before submission. Author guidelines and submission systems change.
:::

## File naming and versioning

Draft manuscripts in Microsoft Word and save them as `.docx` files. Do not use Google Docs. Store and share active manuscripts in the lab's shared OneDrive folder so Shea and the coauthors are working from the same file. Use Word's Track Changes and comments when reviewing or revising a shared draft.

Name each manuscript file using the project name followed by the date in `YYMMDD` format:

```text
[project]-[YYMMDD].docx
```

For example:

```text
ad-biomarkers-260812.docx
```

Create a new dated document after every major revision, including after receiving substantive feedback from Shea or another coauthor. Do not overwrite the previous major version. During a single revision cycle, use tracked changes and comments rather than creating many nearly identical files.

## Page and paragraph formatting

Unless the target journal specifies otherwise:

- Use a sans serif font, such as Arial, in 11- or 12-point type.
- Use 1.5-line spacing for working drafts.
- Justify the main text.
- Use standard 1-inch (2.54-cm) margins.
- Number pages and use continuous line numbering when the target journal requires it; *Alzheimer's & Dementia* requests numbered manuscripts.
- Set paragraph spacing before and after to 0 points.
- Separate paragraphs with one blank line. Do not use paragraph-spacing settings to create the blank line.
- Use the word processor's built-in page breaks and section breaks. Do not press Return repeatedly to move content to a new page.
- Insert page or section breaks between the title page, abstract, main text, references, tables, and figures.

## Headings

Use the [APA heading hierarchy](https://apastyle.apa.org/style-grammar-guidelines/paper-format/headings) for working drafts unless the target journal specifies another system. Use heading levels in order; do not skip from a first-level heading to a third-level heading. Format the heading levels consistently throughout the manuscript.

This preference concerns heading hierarchy and appearance. It does not require APA citation style when the target journal uses a different reference style. *Alzheimer's & Dementia*, for example, generally follows AMA style.

## Tables and figures

- Cite every table and figure in the main text and number each in the order first cited.
- Place tables and figures after the references rather than inline in the main text.
- Start every table and every figure on a new page.
- Keep each table with its title and footnotes.
- Keep each figure with its caption during internal review, unless the target journal requests captions in a separate section or file.
- Confirm that abbreviations, symbols, colors, and sample sizes are defined consistently across the text, tables, figures, and captions.
- At submission, follow the target journal's requirements for separate figure files, resolution, dimensions, color mode, and file type.

## Gene and protein nomenclature

Italicize gene symbols when referring to genes, alleles, or RNA transcripts. Do not italicize protein symbols. For human genes, use the approved symbol listed by the [HUGO Gene Nomenclature Committee](https://www.genenames.org/); the [HGNC guidance](https://www.genenames.org/about/guidelines/) explains the distinction between gene and protein styling. Follow the relevant organism-specific nomenclature authority for nonhuman species.

## Formatting an IMRaD manuscript

Use the target journal's required organization. If no journal has been selected, use the following working structure for an Introduction, Methods, Results, and Discussion (IMRaD) paper:

```text
TITLE PAGE
  Manuscript title
  Authors and affiliations
  Corresponding author and contact information
  Target journal
  Main-text, abstract, table, and figure counts

[PAGE BREAK]

ABSTRACT
  Abstract
  Keywords, if required

[PAGE BREAK]

INTRODUCTION

METHODS

RESULTS

DISCUSSION

[PAGE BREAK]

ACKNOWLEDGMENTS

FUNDING

DATA AND CODE SHARING

[PAGE BREAK]

REFERENCES

[PAGE BREAK]

TABLE 1

[PAGE BREAK]

TABLE 2
  Continue with one table per page

[PAGE BREAK]

FIGURE 1

[PAGE BREAK]

FIGURE 2
  Continue with one figure per page
```

Use descriptive Methods and Results subheadings that align with the study aims and appear in a parallel order. Report findings in Results; reserve interpretation, comparison with prior literature, implications, and limitations for the Discussion.

## Supplementary material

Prepare supplementary material separately from the main manuscript. Unless the target journal requires a different arrangement, use separate documents for:

- supplementary methods and figures; and
- supplementary tables and extended results.

Number supplementary items independently (for example, Table S1 and Figure S1), cite every item in the main manuscript or supplement text, and keep terminology and analysis order consistent with the main paper.

## Use of artificial intelligence

AI tools can help authors check, organize, and revise a manuscript, but they do not replace scientific judgment or author responsibility. Use the [new JAMA guidance on AI use](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/2852772), the [JAMA Instructions for Authors](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/pages/instructions-for-authors#secArtificialIntelligence), and the target journal's current policy as starting points. The target journal's rules take precedence when they are more restrictive.

Follow these lab expectations:

- Do not list an AI tool as an author. Only people can take responsibility for a manuscript.
- Authors remain responsible for the accuracy, originality, integrity, and appropriate citation of every part of the submitted work, including material suggested or edited by AI.
- Independently verify every AI-assisted claim, quotation, statistic, calculation, interpretation, code change, and citation against the primary source or underlying data.
- Do not use AI to generate or format references. Use a reference manager and verify every reference in the cited source. AI tools can invent references or return incorrect bibliographic details.
- Do not upload protected health information, identifiable participant data, confidential or embargoed results, unpublished manuscripts received for peer review, reviewer identities, grant applications, proprietary code, or other restricted material to an AI service unless that use has been explicitly approved for the project and workspace.
- Do not use generative AI to create, alter, or enhance clinical images. If AI-generated or AI-modified content is part of the formal research design, follow the target journal's policy and report the method completely.
- Do not delegate decisions about authorship, scientific conclusions, interpretation of evidence, or responses to reviewers to AI. The authors must make and defend those decisions.
- Retain a brief AI-use log with the tool, model or version, manufacturer, date, purpose, manuscript section, and how the output was checked. Store the log with the manuscript files.

Disclose substantive AI assistance according to the target journal's policy. Current JAMA guidance requires disclosure when AI assists with content creation, revision, or formatting. The disclosure should identify the tool, version, manufacturer, date(s) used, what it did, which parts of the manuscript it affected, and confirmation that the authors take responsibility for the resulting content. Put the disclosure in the Acknowledgments, or in the Methods when AI is part of the research design. JAMA exempts basic grammar and spelling tools, but another journal may not.

If AI is part of the research itself, describe its use with enough detail to reproduce the work and follow the applicable AI reporting guideline. Report the model and version, access date, inputs, prompts or instructions when relevant, parameters, outputs, validation, human oversight, and any changes made after generation. Address privacy, bias, copyright, and intellectual-property concerns explicitly.

## Revisions and resubmissions

Preserve an exact record of every submission round in the manuscript's shared OneDrive folder. Use the following folders:

```text
R0/   Original submission
R1/   First revision
R2/   Second revision
R3/   Third revision, if needed
```

The `R0` folder must contain the exact files sent with the original submission, including the manuscript, cover letter, tables, figures, supplements, reporting checklists, and submission confirmation. Do not edit files in `R0` after submission. Copy the necessary files into `R1` when preparing the first revision. Follow the same process for later rounds so that `R1`, `R2`, and subsequent folders remain exact records of what was submitted in each round.

Each revision folder should contain:

- the editor's decision letter and all reviewer comments;
- a point-by-point response to the editor and reviewers;
- a tracked-changes manuscript;
- a clean revised manuscript;
- revised tables, figures, supplements, checklists, and cover letter, as applicable; and
- the submission confirmation and a copy of every file actually submitted.

Address reviewer comments one at a time and preserve their order. Organize the response by editor and reviewer, number every comment, and reproduce each comment verbatim in bold. Put the response immediately below it in regular, nonbold text. State what changed and give the page and line numbers in the revised manuscript. If no change was made, respond respectfully and explain the scientific or methodological reason.

Use this format:

**Reviewer 1, Comment 1.1: [Paste the reviewer's complete comment here.]**

Response: Thank you for this comment. We revised [brief description of the change].

Location: Page X, lines Y-Z.

**Reviewer 1, Comment 1.2: [Paste the next complete comment here.]**

Response: [Address this comment only.]

Check that every response agrees with the revised manuscript and that every promised change appears in both the clean and tracked versions. Do not mark a comment as addressed until the response, manuscript, tables, figures, and supplements are internally consistent.

## Recommended writing resources

- Yellowlees Douglas and Maria B. Grant, [*The Biomedical Writer: What You Need to Succeed in Academic Medicine*](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/the-biomedical-writer/116D9FE29556A8F2AB5BD408B49AB957) (2018): practical guidance for biomedical manuscripts, grants, collaboration, and publication.
- Yellowlees Douglas, [*Writing for the Reader's Brain: A Science-Based Guide*](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/writing-for-the-readers-brain/26FD3B7599BC12639DFB660F3CA962C8) (2024): a reader-centered framework built around clarity, continuity, coherence, concision, and cadence.
- Stephen B. Heard, [*The Scientist's Guide to Writing: How to Write More Easily and Effectively Throughout Your Scientific Career*, 3rd ed.](https://www.degruyterbrill.com/document/isbn/9780691281094/html?lang=en) (2026): advice on writing habits, manuscript structure, revision, peer review, and journal selection.
- Wendy Laura Belcher, [*Writing Your Journal Article in Twelve Weeks: A Guide to Academic Publishing Success*, 2nd ed.](https://press.uchicago.edu/ucp/books/book/chicago/W/bo26985005) (2019): a structured workbook for developing, revising, and submitting a journal article.

## Final formatting check

Before sending a draft to Shea or submitting it to a journal, and only when permitted by the project and journal policies described under [Use of artificial intelligence](#use-of-artificial-intelligence), run the manuscript through an approved ChatGPT workspace and ask it to audit the document against every item in this guide. Ask for a checklist that identifies each problem and its page, section, table, or figure location. Use ChatGPT to identify problems, not to change scientific claims or silently rewrite the manuscript. Record this use in the AI-use log and disclose it when required by the target journal.

The following prompt can be adapted for the final check:

```text
Audit this manuscript against the Andrews Lab Writing Style Guide.

For every checklist item, report one of the following:
- Pass
- Needs attention, with the page or section and a specific explanation
- Cannot verify in the uploaded file

Check formatting, organization, filename, headings, page and section
breaks, tables, figures, supplements, gene and protein styling,
tracked changes, comments, references, author information,
disclosures, and word counts.

Do not rewrite the manuscript or alter scientific claims. Return only
the audit and recommended corrections.
```

Follow UCSF and project data-handling requirements when using ChatGPT. Do not upload protected, confidential, embargoed, or otherwise restricted material unless its use in the selected ChatGPT workspace has been approved. ChatGPT's audit is a first-pass check; inspect the final document in Microsoft Word before sharing or submission.

Confirm that:

- the manuscript is a Microsoft Word `.docx` file stored in the shared OneDrive folder;
- the filename follows `[project]-[YYMMDD].docx`;
- the target journal and relevant author guidelines are identified;
- headings use a consistent hierarchy;
- font, margins, line spacing, paragraph spacing, and alignment follow the applicable standard;
- page and section breaks are intentional;
- every table, figure, and supplement is cited and numbered in order;
- tables and figures begin on separate pages after the references;
- gene symbols are italicized and protein symbols are not;
- AI use has been logged and disclosed as required, and all AI-assisted content has been verified by an author;
- the correct submission-round folder contains the decision letter, response document, clean and tracked manuscripts, and all revised submission files;
- every editor and reviewer comment has a numbered, point-by-point response and a matching change or rationale;
- all tracked changes, comments, highlights, and placeholders have been resolved as appropriate for the draft stage; and
- spelling, grammar, references, author information, disclosures, and word counts have been checked.
